text: A flood happens when more water arrives than the land can hold or drain away. Usually that water is rain. It soaks into the soil until the soil is full, then it runs over the surface into streams and rivers. When rivers can't carry it all, they spill over their banks.

Some floods build up over days, as a big river slowly rises. Others, called flash floods, arrive in minutes after a cloudburst in hilly country. Along coasts, the sea itself can flood the land when a [[@cyclones-india|cyclone]] pushes it ashore.

sec.t:
On 26 July 2005, a weather station at Santacruz in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] recorded about 944 mm of rain in 24 hours. That is more than London gets in a whole year. Trains stopped, roads became rivers, and many people walked home through water for hours.

The numbers explain why. One centimetre of rain over one square kilometre is about 10,000 tonnes of water. Mumbai got nearly a hundred times that in a day. No drain system on Earth is built for it.

India gets most of its rain in a few months of [[@monsoon|monsoon]], so river floods are a yearly event in places like Assam and Bihar. In [[@assam-tea|Assam]], the [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] floods so often that people on [[@majuli|Majuli]], a river island, build houses raised on bamboo stilts.

Flash floods are different. In June 2013, days of extreme rain fell over the mountains of [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]]. Swollen streams and a burst glacial lake sent a wall of water and boulders down the valley at Kedarnath. Steep slopes leave water no time to soak in, so it rushes downhill, gathering mud and rocks as it goes.

Floods aren't only a disaster. Every time a river spills over, it drops fine mud called silt across the fields. For thousands of years, farmers in Egypt waited for the [[@egypt-nile|Nile]] to flood each summer, because the silt made the soil rich. The great plains of north India and [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] were built the same way.

That changed in Egypt after the Aswan High Dam was finished in 1970. Now the Nile doesn't flood, but farmers must use fertiliser instead. [[@dams-power|Dams]] can hold back floods, but they also trap the silt.

On coasts, the biggest floods often come from the sea. A cyclone's winds can pile ocean water into a dome several metres high, called a storm surge. In 2005, Hurricane Katrina's surge broke the flood walls of [[@new-orleans|New Orleans]] in the USA, and most of the city ended up under water.

In the [[@mississippi|Mississippi]] valley, the Great Flood of 1927 covered land in several states for months. Afterwards the US government built huge walls and spillways along the river, and engineers still argue about how best to let a big river breathe.

text: A hot-air balloon floats because hot air is lighter than cold air. When air is heated, its tiny particles move faster and spread out. So a balloon full of hot air holds fewer particles than the same space filled with cooler air. It weighs less.

The cooler air around the balloon pushes it upwards, the same way water pushes up on a beach ball. This upward push is called buoyancy. If the push is bigger than the weight of the balloon, basket and passengers, the balloon rises. A burner roars above the passengers' heads to keep the air hot.

st.reveal: Winds often blow in different directions at different heights. By heating the air to rise, or letting it cool to sink, a pilot can move into a layer of wind going roughly where they want.

sec.t:
Air is heavier than it seems. A cubic metre of air at about 20 °C weighs about 1.2 kg. Heat it to around 100 °C, and the same space holds only about 0.95 kg. Each cubic metre of hot air can therefore lift roughly 0.25 kg.

That sounds tiny. So balloons have to be huge. To lift a basket, burner, fuel and three or four people, maybe 500 kg in all, you need roughly 2,000 cubic metres of hot air. That's a balloon about as tall as a six-storey building, holding almost as much air as an Olympic swimming pool holds water.

sec.h: A sheep, a duck and a rooster

sec.t:
The pilot controls height with the burner. A blast of flame heats the air and the balloon rises. Let the air cool, or open a vent at the top, and it sinks.

There is no way to steer sideways. The balloon goes wherever the wind blows. But winds often blow in different directions at different heights. A skilled pilot climbs or sinks to find a layer heading roughly the right way. A chase car follows on the ground to collect everyone at the end.

Balloons usually fly just after sunrise or before sunset, when winds are calm and the air is steady.

In 1999, the Swiss balloonist Bertrand Piccard and the British pilot Brian Jones flew all the way around the world without stopping, in about 20 days. Their balloon used both helium and hot air. They rode fast winds high up called [[@jet-streams|jet streams]] for much of the way.

Scientists use balloons too. Every day, weather services in India, the USA and around the world launch hundreds of small [[@weather-balloons|helium balloons carrying instruments]]. They rise through the [[@clouds-types|clouds]] and radio back temperature, wind and moisture for [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]].

Every October, the Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta in New Mexico, USA, fills the sky with hundreds of balloons, some shaped like animals and cartoon characters. It is the biggest balloon festival in the world. The same idea also lifts the paper sky lanterns released at some festivals, although these can start fires and harm animals, so many places now discourage them. The physics is the same as in a huge steel ship that [[@floating-ships|floats]] on water: if something weighs less than the stuff it pushes aside, up it goes.

text: This is called [[photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. It's how almost every [[foodchain|food chain]] on Earth begins.

A leaf takes in carbon dioxide from the air through tiny holes on its surface, and water comes up from the roots. Inside the leaf's cells, a green pigment called [[chlorophyll|chlorophyll]] soaks up sunlight. The plant uses that energy to join carbon dioxide and water into [[@sugar|sugar]], its food. Oxygen is left over and floats out into the air.
That's why [[@extinction|the asteroid]]'s darkness was so deadly: no sunlight, no plant food, no food for anyone.
Tiny ocean plants called plankton make about half of all the oxygen on Earth.

sec.t:
Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light for energy but reflects green. That's why leaves look green. In autumn, some trees stop making chlorophyll and other colours show.

The chlorophyll sits inside tiny green packets in each cell, called chloroplasts. A single leaf can hold millions of them. Seen under a microscope, they look like green beads drifting inside the cells.

In the early 1600s, a Flemish scientist named Jan Baptist van Helmont planted a willow sapling in a big pot of soil that he had dried and weighed. For five years he gave it nothing but rainwater. The willow grew from about 2 kg to about 77 kg. When he dried and weighed the soil again, it had lost only around 60 grams.

He decided the tree was made from water. He was partly right. Later scientists found the missing ingredient. In 1771, the English chemist Joseph Priestley showed that a sprig of mint could "restore" air in a sealed jar, so that a [[@candles|candle]] could burn in it again. A few years later, the Dutch doctor Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants only do this in light, and only in their green parts.

So a giant [[@redwoods|redwood]] or a [[@banyan|banyan]] is built mainly from carbon dioxide pulled out of the air, plus water. The soil supplies only small amounts of minerals.

{{story:sun-what}}

Rice, wheat, fruit, and even milk and meat. All your food energy started as sunlight captured by plants. A cow eats grass, you drink the milk, and the energy in it began in a leaf. The energy in that sunlight began in the [[@sun-what|Sun]], where atoms crash together deep inside.

Fossil fuels such as coal are photosynthesis too, in a way. They are the remains of plants and tiny sea creatures that captured sunlight hundreds of millions of years ago.

Early Earth had almost no oxygen in its air. Then, more than 2.4 billion years ago, tiny ocean microbes called cyanobacteria began using sunlight to make food. They released oxygen as waste, and over hundreds of millions of years it built up in the air. Every animal that breathes, including you, depends on that change.

Today forests, grasslands and crops do a lot of the work on land, but microscopic plankton drifting in the sunlit top of the ocean make about half of the world's oxygen. Some [[@coral-reefs|coral]] even keep tiny algae living inside their bodies, which share the sugar they make.

A [[@solar-panels|solar panel]] also catches sunlight, but it turns it into [[@electricity-made|electricity]], not food. The best panels turn about a fifth of the light into electricity. A typical leaf stores only about 1% of the sunlight that falls on it. The leaf, though, builds and repairs itself, makes its own copies and runs on nothing but air, water and light.

text: A zoo keeps wild animals in enclosures so that people can see them. Good zoos also breed rare animals, do research and teach visitors about nature.

A sanctuary is a place where animals are protected for their own sake. The word means two slightly different things. In India, a *wildlife sanctuary* is a large wild area, like a forest or lake, protected by law, where animals live freely and you might never spot them. Elsewhere, a *sanctuary* often means a rescue centre that gives a lifelong home to animals that cannot survive in the wild, such as injured, orphaned or once-captive animals. Real sanctuaries don't buy, sell or breed animals for show.

Rescue centres for injured animals also call themselves sanctuaries, which is why the word can be confusing.

sec.t:
India's Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 lets governments declare forests, grasslands and [[@wetlands|wetlands]] as sanctuaries or [[@national-parks|national parks]]. India now has over 500 sanctuaries and over 100 national parks. In a sanctuary, local people may sometimes collect firewood or graze cattle. A national park is stricter, with almost no human use allowed.

In the USA, wild areas are protected as national parks, wildlife refuges and wilderness areas. [[@usa-wonder-yellowstone|Yellowstone]], set up in 1872, was the world's first national park and helped save the last wild [[@bison-return|bison]].

Until the 2000s, some performers in India captured sloth bear cubs and trained them to "dance" for coins on the roadside. The practice was illegal, but it continued. Conservation groups worked with the government and the bear handlers' families, helping the families find new jobs. By 2009 the last known [[@bears-india|dancing bears]] had been rescued. Many now live out their lives in sanctuaries such as the bear rescue centre near Agra, where they can dig, climb and forage.

Supporters point to animals saved by zoo breeding, like the Arabian oryx and the California condor. Zoos also raise money for conservation, and for many children a zoo is the first place they see a living tiger.

Critics argue that some animals suffer in captivity however good the enclosure. Big, far-roaming, intelligent animals, such as [[@elephants-talk|elephants]] and polar bears, are hardest to keep well. In 2009, India's Central Zoo Authority directed zoos to move their elephants to forest camps and rescue centres, where they would have more room. The argument about what we owe wild animals is still going on. Many people now agree on one thing: whatever we decide about zoos, protecting animals' wild homes matters most.

text: A gear is a wheel with teeth around its edge. When two gears mesh, the teeth of one push the teeth of the other, so turning one turns the other.

Gears do three useful jobs. They can change speed, making something turn faster or slower. They can change force, making it easier or harder to turn. And they can change direction, because two gears that mesh always turn opposite ways.

The key is size. When a small gear drives a big one, the big one turns more slowly but with more force. When a big gear drives a small one, the small one spins faster but with less force. You can't have both at once.

st.reveal: Each time the small gear turns once, 10 teeth pass, which moves the big gear a quarter of the way round. Four turns of the small gear move 40 teeth, so the big gear turns once. It turns slowly, but with four times the turning force.

sec.t:
Engineers describe gears by their ratio, which you can work out by counting teeth. If a 10-tooth gear drives a 40-tooth gear, the ratio is 1 to 4. The small gear must turn four times to turn the big one once.

In exchange, the big gear turns with four times the force. It works a lot like a [[@lever-lift|lever]]: a long handle lets you lift something heavy, but you have to move your end further. Gears are levers that keep going round and round. The same maths of comparing numbers, called [[@ratios-cooking|ratios]], turns up in recipes, maps and music.

In 1901, sponge divers near the Greek island of Antikythera found a corroded lump of bronze in an old shipwreck. Decades later, X-ray scans revealed what it was: a machine with more than 30 interlocking gears, built about 2,000 years ago.

Turned by a handle, the [[@antikythera|Antikythera mechanism]] showed the positions of the Sun and Moon, the Moon's phases and the dates of eclipses. Nothing as complex has been found from the next thousand years. Every one of its tiny triangular gear teeth was made by hand.

In villages across India and Pakistan, farmers once used the Persian wheel, or *rahat*, to lift water from wells. An ox walked in a circle, turning a horizontal wooden wheel with pegs for teeth. Those pegs turned an upright wheel carrying a loop of pots, which scooped water up and tipped it into a channel. The gears changed the ox's slow, flat circle into a turning wheel standing on its edge.

Mechanical [[@clocks|clocks]] use whole families of gears. One gear turns once a minute for the second hand. A chain of gears slows that down to one turn an hour for the minute hand, and slower again for the hour hand. Gears turning wind turbines, cranes and [[@how-mixer-grinder|food mixers]] all follow the same simple rule of counting teeth.

text: Banknotes are printed on special paper made mostly from cotton, sometimes mixed with linen. In some countries they're printed on thin plastic, called polymer. The paper is made in secure mills, with watermarks and security threads built in while it's still wet pulp.

Then printing presses add layer after layer: background patterns, colour-changing ink, tiny writing, a portrait and serial numbers. Large sheets with dozens of notes each are checked by machines and people, cut into single notes, counted and sent to the central bank. In India, the Reserve Bank of India's notes come from four presses: in Nashik, Dewas, Mysuru and Salboni.

sec.t:
Ordinary paper is made from wood pulp, which turns soft and falls apart when wet. Banknote paper is made from cotton fibres, often from leftovers of cotton mills. Cotton is long and strong, so notes survive pockets, wallets and the occasional wash. The US government says its notes can be folded back and forth about 4,000 times before they tear.

US notes are 75% cotton and 25% linen. India's notes use cotton too, with paper made at mills in Narmadapuram (once called Hoshangabad) and Mysuru. During papermaking, the pulp is pressed thinner in some places and thicker in others, creating a watermark, a picture you can see when you hold the note up to the light. A security thread is woven into the paper at the same time.

sec.h: A thousand years of paper money
sec.t:
The first government paper money was used in China during the Song dynasty, about 1,000 years ago. Merchants in Sichuan had been using paper receipts instead of carrying heavy iron coins, and the government took over printing them. When the traveller Marco Polo visited China in the 1200s, he was astonished that people traded paper for real goods.

India's first paper notes were issued by private banks in the late 1700s. The Reserve Bank of India, set up in 1935, began printing its own notes in 1938.

In 1988, Australia introduced the first polymer notes in wide use, made of a tough plastic film. They're harder to forge and last much longer than cotton notes. Canada, the UK, Singapore and many other countries now use them too.

How long does a note last? The US Federal Reserve estimates a $1 note lasts about 7 years, while a $100 note, used less often, lasts about 23 years. Worn-out notes are shredded. In India, old notes are shredded and sometimes turned into bricks or pressed boards.

In India, many people now pay with phones using [[@upi-payments|UPI]], and in some cities, shopkeepers prefer a QR code to cash. Yet India still prints billions of notes each year, and cash remains important where internet is patchy.

The value of a note doesn't come from the cotton or ink. It comes from trust that others will accept it. If governments print too much, that trust can wobble, and prices climb, a problem economists call [[@inflation|inflation]].

text: Drums are found almost everywhere because they are simple to make and powerful to hear. Stretch an animal skin over a hollow log, a clay pot or a gourd, and strike it. You have a drum. People in every continent worked this out on their own.

Drums also do jobs that matter to people. They keep a group moving together, whether soldiers marching, farmers working or dancers at a wedding. Their low, loud sound travels a long way, so they can send signals. And a steady beat seems to tug at the human body, making us want to tap our feet.

sec.t:
When you hit a drumskin, it bends in and springs back, over and over, very fast. Each push squeezes the air, sending out waves of sound, as you can read in [[@sound-travel|how sound travels]]. A big, loose skin vibrates slowly and booms. A small, tight one vibrates fast and sounds higher.

Most drums vibrate in a jumble of different patterns at once, so they sound like a thump rather than a clear note. Some drums, like the Indian [[@tabla|tabla]], use clever tricks to make the vibrations line up into a ringing musical note.

India has hundreds of kinds of drums. The *dhol*, a big barrel drum played with sticks, powers [[@bhangra|bhangra]] dancing in Punjab and wedding processions everywhere. In Kerala, rows of *chenda* drummers play at [[@india-wonder-thrissur-pooram|temple festivals]], loud enough to feel in your chest.

The *mridangam* keeps rhythm for South Indian classical music. The *damru*, a small hourglass drum, is held by Shiva in Hindu art. In the past, giant *nagara* kettledrums were played at royal palace gates to announce the hours or the arrival of a king.

Before 1900, bands in the USA needed several drummers: one for the bass drum, one for the snare and another for cymbals. Around the early 1900s, drummers in New Orleans and in theatres began playing all of them at once. A foot pedal for the bass drum, made popular from about 1909, freed their hands.

The result was nicknamed the "trap set", short for "contraption". It became the heartbeat of [[@jazz|jazz]], then of rock, pop and [[@hip-hop|hip-hop]]. Today, a drum kit sits at the back of almost every band, from school concerts to stadium shows.

Scientists have found that a steady beat activates parts of the [[@brain-works|brain]] that plan movement, even when you are sitting still. That may be why crowds clap in time at cricket matches, and why marching bands play at [[@american-football|American football]] games.

Drumming together also helps groups feel connected. Around the world, people drum at festivals, prayers, weddings and protests. In the language of drums, there is always a part for everyone, as you can read in [[@rhythm-beat|rhythm]].

text: Pattachitra is a style of painting from [[@odisha|Odisha]], on India's east coast. The name joins two Sanskrit words: *patta*, meaning cloth, and *chitra*, meaning picture. Painters work on specially prepared [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]] cloth, using colours they often make by hand.

The pictures are bold and crowded. Gods and heroes have large eyes and sharp profiles, and every gap is filled with flowers, leaves or tiny patterns. A thick border runs around the edge like a frame. Most paintings tell stories about Lord Jagannath of Puri, Krishna, or scenes from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]].

The traditional canvas is cloth, carefully layered with chalk and gum until it is smooth and stiff. Painters make most of their own colours, and the craft also includes pictures scratched onto palm leaves.

sec.t:
Making the canvas takes days. Painters soak [[@tamarind|tamarind seeds]] and grind them into a sticky gum. They spread it between two layers of old cotton cloth so the layers stick together. Once dry, the cloth is coated with a paste of chalk and gum, then rubbed smooth with a stone.

The result is stiff and slightly shiny, a little like thick card. It can hold fine lines without the paint soaking in or spreading.

Preparing canvas has traditionally been shared work in painter families. Some members prepare the cloth and grind colours, while the most skilled hands draw the fine lines and faces. A large painting can take weeks, and a very detailed one can take months.

Pattachitra grew up around the Jagannath temple in Puri. Every summer, after a grand bathing festival, the temple's three deities are said to fall ill. For about two weeks they are hidden from view while they recover. During this time, called *anasara*, worshippers pray before painted images of the gods instead.

Painters also sold small pictures to pilgrims as souvenirs to carry home, long before postcards existed. The temple and its yearly chariot festival, the Rath Yatra, are still favourite subjects. Jagannath, with his round eyes and broad smile, is easy to recognise even in a tiny painting, so he appears on everything from wall hangings to bookmarks.

Raghurajpur, a short drive from Puri, is a village where many families make Pattachitra. Houses have painted walls, and children often learn by helping their parents. Visitors can watch the whole process, from tamarind paste to finished painting. The Odisha government has developed it as a heritage crafts village.

The same artists often make *tala pattachitra*, where a design is scratched onto dried palm leaves with an iron stylus and then rubbed with soot so the lines show black. Some palm-leaf pieces fold out like a fan or a tiny book.

Neighbouring Bengal has its own scroll tradition, with a similar name. There, painters called *patuas* unroll long vertical scrolls one picture at a time while singing the story, a bit like a hand-drawn [[@comics-art|comic]] performed live.

text: Taxes are money that people and businesses pay to the government. The government uses it to pay for things that everyone shares and that would be hard to buy alone: roads, schools, hospitals, police, the army, clean water, streetlights and space programmes.

You could not easily buy your own highway or hire your own fire brigade. When crores of people each pay a share, the country can afford them together. Taxes also help pay for [[@pensions-old-age|pensions]] for the elderly, free school meals and help after floods and earthquakes.

st.reveal: In India, the price printed on a packet already includes Goods and Services Tax. In most US states, it works the other way, with sales tax added on at the till, so the price you pay is higher than the price tag.

Almost everyone pays some tax. Income tax is paid mainly by people who earn above a certain amount, but taxes on goods, like GST in India or sales tax in the USA, are paid by anyone who buys things, including children.

sec.h: Taxes you see and taxes you don't
sec.t:
Some taxes are paid directly. Income tax is taken from what people earn, and richer people usually pay a bigger share of their income. Companies pay tax on their profits.

Other taxes are hidden inside prices. India's Goods and Services Tax, or GST, began on 1 July 2017. It replaced a tangle of separate state and central taxes with one system. Different goods carry different rates, shown as [[@percentages|percentages]]. In India GST is included in the price you see. In most of the United States, sales tax is added at the till, and it varies by state. A few states, such as Oregon and Delaware, have no statewide sales tax at all.

In 1696, England introduced a window tax. Houses with more windows paid more, on the idea that bigger houses had more windows. Many owners simply bricked some up. Doctors later complained that dark, airless homes made people ill, and the tax was abolished in 1851.

Every February, India's Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in Parliament. It lists how much the government expects to collect and how it plans to spend it, on things like defence, railways, farming, health and [[@roads-built|roads]]. A [[@budget-government|budget]] works much like a family's monthly plan, just with far more zeros. You can learn how to make one in [[@budgets|budgets]].

India's modern income tax began in 1860, when the British introduced it to pay debts after the [[@revolt-1857|revolt of 1857]]. In the United States, a federal income tax became permanent after the 16th Amendment to the Constitution in 1913. Americans file their returns each spring, usually by 15 April.

Nobody enjoys paying taxes, and people disagree strongly about how much tax is fair and what it should be spent on. Some want lower taxes and a smaller government. Others want higher taxes to pay for more public services. Those disagreements are a big part of what elections are about. Most people do agree on one thing: a country where nobody paid tax would have no schools, roads or hospitals for anyone.

text: India has loved comics for decades. In the 1960s and 1970s, children read American heroes such as the Phantom and Mandrake in Indrajal Comics, printed by the Times of India group from 1964. Then came Indian creations: *Amar Chitra Katha* retold myths and history, *Chacha Chaudhary* solved problems with his quick brain, and *[[@tinkle|Tinkle]]* [[@childrens-magazines|filled magazines]] with Suppandi and Shikari Shambu.

In the 1980s and 1990s, Raj Comics brought Indian superheroes such as Nagraj and Super Commando Dhruva. Many of these characters are still in print, now also in apps, cartoons and films. To learn how comics are drawn, see [[@comics-art|the art of comics]].

Reading comics means following words and pictures together, keeping track of time between panels and working out what is left unsaid. Teachers and librarians around the world now use comics to help children enjoy reading.

sec.h: A quiz that started a company
sec.t:
In 1967, Anant Pai, an editor in Bombay, watched [[@tv-quiz-shows|a TV quiz]] from Delhi. The students knew the answers about Greek myths but could not say who Rama's mother was. Pai decided Indian children needed their own stories in a form they enjoyed.

He started *Amar Chitra Katha*, which means "immortal picture stories". At first the series printed Western [[@fairy-tales|fairy tales]], but from 1969 it focused on Indian epics, gods, saints, kings and freedom fighters. Children called Pai "Uncle Pai".

Anant Pai also founded *Tinkle* magazine in 1980. It mixed comics with puzzles, science facts and stories. Its best-known character, Suppandi, is a servant who takes every instruction literally. Shikari Shambu is a hunter who is terrified of animals but somehow always ends up a hero.

Tinkle often printed ideas sent in by readers, so a child in Pune or Patna might see their own joke turned into a comic. Stories from the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]] and tales of [[@akbar-birbal|Akbar and Birbal]] also appeared often in its pages.

In the 1980s, Raj Comics, based in Delhi, created a wave of Indian superheroes. [[@myths-indian-creatures|Nagraj]], the "snake king", first appeared in 1986 and can release tiny snakes from his body. Super Commando Dhruva, who began in 1987, has no superpowers at all. He relies on training, science and his ability to talk to animals.

These comics were sold at railway station bookstalls and lent out by small "comic libraries" for a few rupees a day. Children swapped them, collected them and argued over who was strongest. They borrowed ideas from American [[@superheroes-history|superheroes]] but gave them Indian cities and Indian myths.

Fewer comics are sold on paper than in the 1980s, but many have moved online. New Indian [[@graphic-novels|graphic novels]] for older readers tell stories about history, cities and everyday life. Some cartoonists post comics on [[@social-media|social media]] and gather huge followings.

Old favourites still sell too. Parents who grew up with *Amar Chitra Katha* and *Tinkle* now buy them for their children, and the jokes about Suppandi still land.

text: Your body fights germs in layers. The first layer keeps them out: your [[@skin|skin]], [[@gross-snot|the sticky mucus in your nose]], the [[@eyes-tears|tears]] in your eyes and the acid in your stomach. Most germs never get past these.

When some do, white [[@blood|blood]] cells rush in. Some of them gobble up anything that looks foreign. Others build exact weapons for each new germ, called [[antibody|antibodies]], which stick to the germ and mark it for destruction. Once the fight is won, a few of these cells stay behind for years, remembering. That's why you rarely catch the same illness twice. Together, all these parts are called the immune system.

options.t: Some immune cells remember the germ and attack it fast next time
The chickenpox germ dies out everywhere once you've had it

st.reveal: After an infection, your body keeps memory cells that recognise that exact germ. If it comes back, they raise an army so quickly that you usually don't fall ill at all. Vaccines use the same trick.

The immune system isn't a muscle you can pump up, and an overactive one causes problems like allergies. Sleep, ordinary healthy food, exercise and vaccines help it work the way it should.

sec.t:
Think of your body as a fort. Your skin is the outer wall, made of tough, dead cells packed tightly together. Openings like the nose, mouth and eyes are guarded too. Mucus traps dust and germs, and tiny hairs sweep it away. Tears and saliva contain a chemical that breaks open some bacteria.

Even the [[@microbes-friendly|friendly microbes]] on your skin and in your gut help. They take up space and food, leaving less room for harmful germs. A cut or a scrape is a hole in the wall, which is why the body rushes to seal it with a scab.

The second team is slower but sharper. Cells called B cells make antibodies that fit one particular germ the way a key fits a lock. T cells hunt down your own cells that have been taken over by a virus and destroy them. It takes days to build these weapons the first time, and that is often when you feel most ill.

Antibodies are shaped like the letter Y. The two arms grab the germ, and the stem works like a flag that tells the eating cells where to bite. Your body can make billions of different antibody shapes, so there is usually one that fits even a germ it has never met before.

These cells gather in small lumps called lymph nodes, in your neck, armpits and elsewhere. When you have a sore throat, you might feel swollen bumps under your jaw. Those are lymph nodes busy making an army.

After the fight, most of the new soldiers die off, but some memory cells live on, sometimes for a lifetime. If the same germ returns, they recognise it at once and strike before it can spread.

Some germs keep changing their outer coats, so memory cells don't recognise them. Flu viruses do this, which is why flu [[@vaccines|vaccines]] are updated every year. Colds come from more than 200 different viruses, so beating one doesn't protect you from the next. The immune system can also make mistakes and attack harmless things, as in [[@allergies|allergies]], or even the body itself.

text: You can't skip sleep for ever. Your brain will take it, whether you agree or not. After a day or two without sleep, people get grumpy, clumsy and forgetful. After several days, they start falling asleep for a few seconds at a time without noticing, and some begin to see things that aren't there.

Scientists think sleep lets the brain sort memories, repair itself and clear away waste. Nobody has tested how long a person could go with no sleep at all, because it would be dangerous. The best-recorded attempt, by a teenager in 1964, ended after 11 days.

sec.t:
In December 1963, Randy Gardner, a 17-year-old in San Diego, decided to break the record for staying awake for his school science fair. Friends kept him moving with basketball and car rides. A sleep researcher from Stanford University, William Dement, came to watch.

By day four, Randy thought a street sign was a person. Later he struggled to count backwards from 100 and forgot what he was saying halfway through sentences. He stopped at about 264 hours, or 11 days. Then he slept for about 14 hours and recovered.

Guinness World Records later stopped accepting attempts to stay awake, because they are too risky.

sec.h: What goes wrong, hour by hour
sec.t:
After about 24 hours awake, your reactions slow down as much as if you were very tired after a long journey. Your mood drops.

After two or three days, the brain starts grabbing tiny naps called microsleeps. They last a few seconds. You might be staring at a page and not know you've switched off. This is why tired drivers are so dangerous.

Longer than that, [[@memory|memory]] gets patchy, speech gets muddled and people may see shapes in the corners of their eyes.

{{story:sleep-why}}

sec.h: The night shift inside your head
sec.t:
In 2013, scientists at the University of Rochester in the USA watched the brains of sleeping mice. They found fluid flowing faster between brain cells during sleep, washing out waste chemicals. It's a bit like the cleaning crew who come into a school once everyone has gone home.

Sleep also seems to be when the brain sorts the day. Things you practised, from times tables to a cricket shot, are often better the morning after. Some of this happens during [[@dreams|dreams]].

Sleep also helps you grow. Much of the growth hormone your body makes each day is released in deep sleep, early in the night. Your immune system works better after a good night too. People who are short of sleep catch colds more easily, which is one reason doctors tell sick children to rest.

No animal studied has been found to need no sleep at all, but some find clever ways to fit it in. Dolphins rest one half of their brain at a time, so the other half can steer them up to breathe.

Frigatebirds, which glide over the ocean for weeks, take naps of a few seconds while flying. Common swifts may stay in the air for ten months, and scientists believe they sleep on the wing too.

Doctors in the USA recommend 9 to 12 hours a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers. Many children in both India and America get less, thanks to early school buses, tuition classes and screens at night.

If you feel tired all the time, it's worth talking to a parent or doctor. By the time you are ten, you have spent around four years of your life asleep. That sounds like a waste, until you find out what [[@sleep-why|your brain was busy doing]] all that time.

text: Most robots in homes today do one job, and do it over and over. Robot vacuum cleaners are by far the most common. Others mop floors, mow lawns, scrub swimming pools and clean windows. Some toys and learning kits are robots too.

What makes them robots, and not just machines, is that they sense the world, decide what to do and then act on their own. [[@ceiling-fans|A ceiling fan]] spins whether or not someone is under it. A robot vacuum notices a chair leg and steers around it. That loop of sensing, deciding and moving is the basic idea behind every [[@robots|robot]].

It weighs the floor in front of it before rolling forward

st.reveal: Small "cliff sensors" under the front shine invisible infrared light at the floor. If the light doesn't bounce back quickly, there's no floor there, so the robot stops and turns.

sec.h: The disc that learned the house

sec.t:
In 1920, the Czech writer Karel Čapek wrote a play called *R.U.R.* about factory-made workers who eventually rebel. He called them robots, a word his brother Josef suggested. It comes from the Czech *robota*, meaning forced or dull labour.

That origin is a good fit for today's home robots. They take on the [[@life-chores-world|chores]] nobody enjoys: sweeping under the bed, trimming grass in the afternoon heat, scrubbing algae off pool walls.

Čapek's robots were made of something like flesh, not metal. The clanking metal robot came later, from films, comics and magazine covers. Real home robots look like neither. Most are low and round so they can slide under beds, and lawn robots look more like small turtles than people.

sec.h: Why there's no robot butler yet
sec.t:
Here is an odd truth. Computers beat world [[@chess-india|chess]] champions in 1997, yet picking up a sock and folding a shirt remain hard for robots. Researchers noticed this long ago. Skills that feel effortless to people, like seeing, grasping and balancing, took millions of years of evolution and turn out to be very difficult to program.

A shirt can crumple into endless shapes. A plate can be wet, heavy or slippery. Your [[@brain-works|brain]] handles these surprises without you thinking. A robot has to be shown, or trained on huge amounts of practice, and still drops things.

Cost matters too. A robot vacuum is cheap because it only needs wheels, a brush, a few sensors and a small chip. A robot with two arms, fingers and cameras needs dozens of motors, and every one of them can break. In many Indian homes, a family member or a paid helper still does the jobs a robot cannot.

sec.h: Robots that talk, and robots that listen
sec.t:
Smart speakers can answer questions and switch on lights, but most engineers wouldn't call them robots, because they cannot move. Many homes now link lights, locks and [[@how-fridges-cold|fridges]] together on the [[@internet-of-things|Internet of Things]], which lets a robot vacuum start cleaning when everyone leaves.

Companies in the US, China, Japan and India are testing humanoid robots with arms and legs for homes. A few are already sold to researchers. For now, the robot most families own is still the humble disc under the sofa, patiently learning where the furniture lives.

text: The [[@space-station|International Space Station]] has been home to astronauts since 2000, but it is getting old. NASA and its partners plan to retire it around 2030. After that, low Earth orbit will probably have several smaller stations instead of one giant one.

China already has its own station, Tiangong. India plans the Bharatiya Antariksh Station, with a first module targeted for 2028. American companies are building private stations that could host scientists, tourists and astronauts from many countries. Further ahead, engineers dream of spinning stations with artificial gravity, and outposts near the Moon.

sec.h: The ISS, a hard act to follow
sec.t:
The ISS is about as long as a football field and weighs over 400 tonnes. It was built from more than 40 launches by the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. People have lived aboard without a break since November 2000.

But its oldest parts have been in space since 1998, and some are cracking and leaking. Maintenance costs NASA billions of dollars a year. When its time comes, a SpaceX vehicle will dock and fire its engines to slow it down. Most of the station will burn up, and the remaining pieces will fall into a remote stretch of the South Pacific far from any land.

Tiangong, meaning "heavenly palace", was completed in 2022. It is T-shaped, with three main modules, and much smaller and lighter than the ISS. Chinese astronauts, called taikonauts, live there in crews of three, swapping every six months or so. China has invited scientists from other countries to fly experiments aboard. If the ISS retires on schedule, Tiangong may for a while be the only government-run station in orbit.

{{story:space-station}}

India wants its own station too. The Bharatiya Antariksh Station is planned to start with one module launched around 2028, growing to five modules by about 2035. It will build on [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]], India's programme to launch astronauts on Indian rockets.

In 2025, Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla of the Indian Air Force spent about 18 days on the ISS during a private mission called Axiom-4. He was the first Indian to visit the station, and only the second Indian citizen in space, after Rakesh Sharma in 1984. Experience like his will help plan India's station.

NASA no longer wants to own a station. Instead, it plans to rent space on stations built by companies. Several are in the works. Vast, a Californian company, plans a small one-module station called Haven-1, now expected in 2027. Axiom Space wants to attach modules to the ISS and later fly them free. Others, such as Starlab and Orbital Reef, are on drawing boards.

These stations will be cheaper partly because of [[@reusable-rockets|reusable rockets]], which bring launch costs down. They might host film shoots, factories making special medicines or crystals, and paying visitors.

Long stays in weightlessness weaken muscles and bones, so astronauts exercise for about two hours a day. One fix is artificial gravity. In the 1950s, the rocket engineer Wernher von Braun drew a wheel-shaped station that spun to press astronauts gently against its outer rim. The 1968 film *2001: A Space Odyssey* made the idea famous.

A spinning wheel needs to be large, perhaps hundreds of metres wide, or the spin makes people dizzy. Nobody has built one yet. But as rockets get cheaper and bigger, engineers are again sketching wheels, inflatable modules and even stations made from material dug up on the Moon. Future stations may also have to dodge more and more [[@space-junk|space junk]], another problem left for the next generation of builders.

text: Yes, in a way. AI programs can now produce paintings, drawings and photo-like images in seconds. Type "a tiger reading a newspaper on a Mumbai local train, painted like a Mughal miniature", and a few seconds later you get a picture.

These programs have studied hundreds of millions of images, along with the words people used to describe them. From that, they learned which shapes, colours and textures go with which words. When you type a prompt, they build a brand new image to match.
Whether the AI is painting in the way a human artist does is a different question. It has no eyes, no hands and no feelings about the picture. That is one reason AI art is so hotly argued about.

st.reveal: These tools, called diffusion models, start from random static. Step by step, they remove the noise in a way that matches your words, until a picture appears. They learned to do this by practising on millions of images.

myth: AI art programs cut and paste pieces of other people's pictures together, like a collage.

Most build a new image from patterns they learned, rather than gluing clips together. But because they learn from real artworks, they can sometimes produce something very close to an existing picture or an artist's style.

sec.t:
Computer art is older than most people think. In the early 1970s, the British painter Harold Cohen began writing a program called AARON. It could draw shapes, plants and people by following rules Cohen wrote. He kept improving it for over 40 years, and it later learned to colour its own drawings.

But AARON knew only what Cohen taught it. Modern AI is different. It learns from examples on its own, using [[@ai-what|neural networks]] loosely inspired by the brain.

sec.h: Making a picture out of static
sec.t:
Many of today's image tools use a method called diffusion. In training, the AI is shown millions of pictures that have been gradually covered in random speckles, like TV static, until nothing is left. It practises undoing that noise, step by step.

Once trained, it can start from pure static and "clean" it into a new image, guided by your words. A picture is just a grid of coloured dots called [[@pixels|pixels]], so the AI is really deciding the colour of millions of dots, over and over.

AI used to be famously bad at hands, often giving people six or seven fingers. Hands are hard because they bend in so many ways and are often half hidden in photos. Newer tools have improved a lot.

{{story:art-forgery}}

In 2018, the auction house Christie's sold a portrait made with AI by a group of French artists, called Portrait of Edmond de Belamy, for 432,500 US dollars. That was more than 40 times the top price experts had expected.

In 2022, a man in the USA won first prize in the digital art category of the Colorado State Fair with an image made using an AI tool. Some artists were furious. He argued that he had spent many hours choosing words and adjusting the result.

In 2024, a painting made by a humanoid robot called Ai-Da sold for more than a million dollars at Sotheby's.

AI tools learned from huge numbers of images posted online, including the work of living artists, usually without asking them. Many artists say this is unfair, especially when AI can copy their style in seconds. Some have taken AI companies to court.

In the USA, the Copyright Office says an image made entirely by AI, without real human creative choices, cannot be protected by copyright. A US court agreed in 2025. Pictures where a human makes many of the creative decisions are a greyer area.

AI images can look real, which makes them easy to misuse, for example in fake news photos. Clues include odd hands, melted-looking text in the background, earrings that do not match and lighting that makes no sense. Some companies now add hidden labels to AI images to mark where they came from.

Art experts have dealt with fakes for centuries. The tricks used to catch a forged old painting, such as checking paints and brushstrokes, are now joined by new tools that hunt for traces of AI. And the same kind of AI that paints from noise has learned to [[@tech-ai-music|compose music]] too.

text: Archaeologists find out about the past by studying the things people left behind: buildings, tools, pots, bones, seeds and rubbish. Much of human history happened before writing, or in places where writing did not survive. Objects are often the only evidence.

They dig carefully, layer by layer, and record exactly where each object lies. The order of the layers tells them what came first. Historians, who mostly study [[@history-sources|written sources]], often work alongside them. Archaeologists use science to date objects, test what people ate and even where they grew up. Bit by bit, broken pieces become a story.

st.prompt: Archaeologists digging an old city find a layer of ash with broken pots above it and below it. What does the ash layer most likely show?

options.t: A big fire, after which people rebuilt and kept living there
That people stopped using pots
That the pots below are newer than those above

st.reveal: Layers build up over time, with the oldest at the bottom. Pots below the ash were used before the fire, and pots above it after. The ash is a dated "page" in the city's story.

myth: Archaeologists dig up dinosaur bones.

Dinosaurs are studied by palaeontologists. Archaeologists study humans and the things people left behind. The last dinosaurs died out about 6.6 crore years ago, more than 6 crore years before the first humans appeared.
facts: things people made, used and left behind

sec.t:
Over time, dust, mud and rubbish build up on the ground. People build new houses on top of old ones. This creates layers, a bit like pages stacked in a pile. Usually, the deeper the layer, the older it is. Studying layers is called stratigraphy.

That is why archaeologists don't just grab interesting objects. A pot is useful, but knowing which layer it came from, and what lay next to it, tells much more. Once something is dug up, its exact place can never be checked again, so diggers draw, photograph and measure everything.

Some of archaeologists' favourite finds are rubbish heaps. Broken pots, animal bones and burnt seeds show what people cooked and ate. Tiny grains of pollen show what plants grew nearby.

Bones and teeth hold clues too. Unlike [[@fossils-form|fossils]], which have turned to stone over millions of years, the bones archaeologists study are usually only hundreds or thousands of years old. Chemical traces in tooth enamel can show where a person spent their childhood, which helps track how people moved.

In the 1920s, digs at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, now in Pakistan, revealed the [[@indus-cities|Indus civilisation]], with planned streets, brick houses and [[@oddity-ancient-toilets|drains]], more than 4,500 years old. Until then, nobody knew it had existed.

Later finds include Lothal in Gujarat, with what may be an ancient dockyard, and Rakhigarhi in Haryana, one of the largest Indus sites. At Keeladi in Tamil Nadu, recent digs have found pottery with early Tamil writing. The Archaeological Survey of India, founded in 1861, looks after thousands of protected monuments.

Today some archaeology starts in the air. [[@lasers|Lasers]] fired from aircraft, called lidar, can see through forest to the shape of the ground below. In 2018, lidar revealed tens of thousands of hidden Maya structures in the jungles of Guatemala, adding to the list of [[@lost-cities|lost cities]] found again. Ground-penetrating radar can find walls under fields without any digging.

Even so, much of the work still happens on hands and knees with a small trowel and a soft brush, one thin layer at a time. Some finds are pure luck, like the farmers in China whose well-digging struck a clay soldier's head.

text: The Buddha was a teacher who lived in north India around 2,500 years ago. He was born Siddhartha Gautama, a prince of the Shakya people, at Lumbini in what is now [[@nepal|Nepal]].

At 29 he left his comfortable life to search for an end to suffering. After years of searching, he reached what Buddhists call enlightenment, a complete understanding of life, while meditating under a tree at [[@bodh-gaya|Bodh Gaya]] in Bihar. From then on he was called the Buddha, meaning "the awakened one". He spent about 45 years walking across [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]] plains, teaching anyone who would listen. His teachings became Buddhism, one of the world's major religions.

st.prompt: Before his enlightenment, Siddhartha tried eating almost nothing for years. What did he decide about it?

options.t: It didn't work, and a middle way between luxury and hardship was better
Fasting was the only path to wisdom
Food should be shared only with monks

st.reveal: Stories say he became so thin he could barely stand, yet he was no wiser. He accepted a bowl of rice and milk and chose a "Middle Way". Soon after, sitting under a tree at Bodh Gaya, he reached enlightenment.

d.try: Sit quietly for three minutes and simply count your breaths, from one to ten, then start again. Notice how often your mind wanders to something else. Many Buddhists practise this kind of quiet attention every day.
myth: The Buddha is a god whom Buddhists pray to for favours.
The Buddha taught that he was a human being who had woken up to the truth. Buddhists honour him as a teacher and follow his path, though customs vary a lot between countries.
facts: at Bodh Gaya, under a pipal tree

sec.t:
According to tradition, Siddhartha's father kept him inside the palace so he would never see anything sad. One day, out riding, the prince saw an old man, a sick man and a dead body. For the first time he understood that everyone grows old, falls ill and dies.

Then he saw a calm wandering monk. That sight gave him an idea. He left his wife, his baby son and his riches, and set out to find a way beyond suffering.

Historians can't check this story, and it may be a teaching tale more than a diary of events. But it captures something people across Asia have found powerful: a rich young man realising that money cannot protect anyone from growing old.

At a deer park in Sarnath, near [[@varanasi|Varanasi]], the Buddha gave his first teaching to five companions. He explained the Four Noble Truths: life includes suffering; suffering comes from craving; it can end; and there is a path to end it.

That path is the Eightfold Path. It includes right speech, right action, right effort and right [[@mindfulness|mindfulness]], among others. He taught kindness towards all living beings. He welcomed people of any [[@caste-history|caste]] into his community of monks, and later he accepted women as nuns too.

The Buddha died at about 80 at Kushinagar, in today's Uttar Pradesh. His followers divided his ashes and built stupas over them.

About 200 years later, Emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]] visited Lumbini and set up a stone pillar there. Its inscription says, in effect, "Here the Buddha was born". It is one of the strongest pieces of evidence that the Buddha was a real person in a real place.

Buddhism spread from India to [[@sri-lanka|Sri Lanka]], Tibet, China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia. Monks carried texts along trade routes, and great monasteries like [[@nalanda|Nalanda]] drew students from across Asia.

Over the centuries, Buddhism faded in India, though it never vanished. In 1956, B.R. Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of his followers became Buddhists in Nagpur, giving it new life. Today about 32 crore people call themselves Buddhists (a 2020 estimate), and many more follow some of his teachings alongside other traditions. Most of them live in East and Southeast Asia.

text: The Delhi Sultanate was a series of Muslim kingdoms that ruled much of north India from Delhi between 1206 and 1526. Its rulers were called sultans.

Five dynasties held power one after another: the Mamluks (sometimes called the Slave dynasty), the Khaljis, the Tughlaqs, the Sayyids and the Lodis. At its largest, under the Khaljis and the Tughlaqs, the sultanate reached deep into south India. The period brought new styles of building with arches and domes, new kinds of music and poetry, and a new mixed language that grew into [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] and [[@urdu|Urdu]]. It ended in 1526, when Babur defeated the last sultan at Panipat and founded the [[@mughals|Mughal]] Empire.

st.prompt: Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued copper and brass coins that were meant to be worth as much as silver ones. What happened?

options.t: People made fake coins at home, and the plan collapsed
Everyone happily used them for 200 years
Silver became worthless overnight

st.reveal: The new coins were easy to copy, so many people made their own and paid taxes with them. The treasury filled with fakes. The sultan had to buy back the coins with real silver and gold, and huge heaps of them piled up near his fort.

It was five separate dynasties, some lasting only a few decades. Power often changed hands through rebellions and murders at court.

sec.h: A slave who became a king
sec.t:
The first sultan, Qutb-ud-din Aibak, began life as an enslaved soldier. In Central Asia at that time, slaves were often trained as soldiers and officials, and some rose very high. Aibak became a general for the ruler Muhammad of Ghor, and took charge of his Indian lands.

Around 1199, Aibak began building the Qutb Minar in [[@delhi|Delhi]], a tower of red and buff sandstone. His successor, Iltutmish, finished it. At about 73 metres, it is as tall as a 24-storey building, and it is now a UNESCO [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage]] Site.

sec.h: Razia, the sultan who was a woman

sec.t:
Alauddin Khalji, who ruled from 1296 to 1316, faced repeated invasions by [[@mongols|Mongol]] armies from Central Asia. To pay a large standing army, he fixed the prices of grain, cloth and horses in Delhi's markets, and punished shopkeepers who cheated on weights.

His armies also marched south and brought back great wealth. Court historians praised his control, while others recorded that people found his rule harsh. He was one of the few rulers of the time to keep the Mongols out of India.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq, who ruled from 1325 to 1351, was clever and well read, yet many of his plans failed. In 1327 he ordered the capital moved from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan, about 1,100 km away. Many people suffered on the march, and the court later returned.

He also issued copper and brass token coins to stand in for silver, an idea a bit like modern [[@money-worth|money]]. But they were easy to forge, and the plan collapsed. The Moroccan traveller [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] worked for him as a judge and described his generosity and his sudden anger.

The next sultan, Firoz Shah Tughlaq, built canals, gardens and towns. He also had two of [[@ashoka|Ashoka]]'s ancient stone pillars carried to Delhi, wrapped in silk cotton and moved on a huge cart.

The poet and musician Amir Khusrau lived in this era. He wrote in Persian and in Hindavi, an early form of Hindi and Urdu, and he is linked to the growth of [[@qawwali|qawwali]] [[@singing|singing]]. In 1398, the Central Asian conqueror Timur sacked Delhi, and the sultanate never fully recovered. In 1526, Babur's guns and cavalry defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, and a new empire began.

text: The first film show with a paying audience, the kind most people mean by "the first film", happened in Paris on 28 December 1895. Two brothers from France, Auguste and Louis Lumière, projected ten short films onto a screen in a basement room called the Salon Indien, below the Grand Café.

Each film was under a minute long. One showed workers leaving a factory, another a baby being fed, another a gardener getting sprayed by his own hose. About 33 people paid one franc to watch. Within weeks, queues stretched down the street.

st.prompt: What was the very first film the Lumière brothers ever made and showed?

options.t: Workers leaving their factory at lunchtime
A train rushing at the audience
A magician making things disappear

st.reveal: Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory shows people streaming out of the brothers' factory gates in Lyon. It is under a minute long and has no story at all, yet audiences were thrilled to see real people move on a screen.

src: Institut Lumière, Lyon, history of the Cinématographe.

Library of Congress, Edison Motion Pictures.
n.certNote: Which film counts as "first" depends on the rules. Louis Le Prince filmed moving pictures in 1888, Edison showed films in peep-show boxes from 1893, and the Skladanowsky brothers projected films in Berlin weeks before the Lumières.

d.try: Make a flipbook. Take a small notepad and draw a stick figure on the last page. On each page going forward, draw it again, moved a tiny bit. Flip the pages fast with your thumb and watch it move, just as film does with still pictures.
myth: When the Lumières first showed a train arriving at a station, the audience screamed and ran out of the room.
There is no reliable report of this from the time. The story appeared years later and grew with each telling. The train film was not even part of the first public programme.

sec.t:
The Lumières were not the first to capture moving pictures. In 1888, a French inventor named Louis Le Prince filmed his family walking in a garden in Leeds, England. That clip, about 2 seconds long, is the oldest surviving moving picture.

In the USA, Thomas Edison's team built the Kinetoscope, a wooden cabinet with a peephole. From 1893, one person at a time could watch a short film inside. In Berlin, the Skladanowsky brothers projected films for an audience on 1 November 1895, weeks before Paris. Their machine was clumsy, though, and the Lumières' design spread round the world.

On 7 July 1896, a cameraman working for the Lumières showed six films at Watson's Hotel in Bombay. Newspapers in the city wrote about it with excitement. Tickets cost one rupee, a lot of money then. Soon films were shown in tents, theatres and fairgrounds across India.

Watching those early shows inspired Indians to make their own. In 1913, [[@dadasaheb-phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]] released *Raja Harishchandra*, India's first full-length feature film. Because women didn't act on stage then, men played the female roles.

The film everyone remembers is *Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat*, shot in 1895 and shown in 1896. The train steams towards the camera at an angle, growing bigger until it fills the screen. A famous story says people ran screaming out of the room. Historians have found no real evidence of this, but the film did show how powerful a moving image could be.

The Lumières sent camera operators all over the world to film and show films, including to India, Egypt, Japan, Mexico and the USA. Each operator carried a Cinématographe, shot local scenes, developed the film and showed it the same week. Many of the earliest moving images of cities like Cairo, Moscow and New York were taken this way, and some can still be watched online.

sec.h: From 20 minutes to a giant industry
sec.t: Within ten years, filmmakers were telling stories, adding special effects and building studios. Today India makes more films than any other country, often well over 1,500 a year, and Hollywood earns billions. All of it grew from ten tiny films in a café basement. The brothers themselves soon went back to photography. A famous line has the Lumière family calling cinema "an invention without a future". Nobody is sure who really said it, and the people who built [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] went on to prove the opposite.

text: The Smithsonian Institution is a group of museums, a zoo and research centres run for the people of the United States. Most of its museums stand along the National Mall, the long grassy park in the middle of [[@washington-dc|Washington, DC]], and all of those are free to enter.

Between them they hold nearly 157 million things. There are dinosaur bones, moon rocks, aeroplanes, paintings, the flag that inspired the American national anthem and a pair of ruby slippers from a famous film. Most of the collection, about 148 million items, is scientific specimens like insects, fossils and minerals kept at the natural history museum. Only a tiny share is ever on display.

In an armoured truck with police guards

st.reveal: He mailed it, using registered post with insurance. A postman delivered one of the world's most famous jewels, and the wrapping is still kept in the collection.

myth: The Smithsonian is one big museum.
It's a group of 21 museums, a zoo and several research centres. Most sit along the National Mall in Washington, but a few are in New York, Virginia and elsewhere.

sec.t:
James Smithson was a British chemist who studied minerals. When he died in 1829, his will said that if his nephew died without children, his fortune should go to the United States "to found at Washington... an establishment for the increase and diffusion of knowledge". Nobody knows exactly why. He had never visited.

The nephew died in 1835. In 1838 the money crossed the Atlantic as 105 bags of gold coins. Congress then argued for eight years about what to do with it, before setting up the Smithsonian in 1846. Its first building, a red sandstone castle with towers, still stands on the Mall. Smithson's remains were moved there in 1904.

Some Smithsonian museums tell the history of particular people. The National Museum of the American Indian shows art and objects from Native nations across the Americas. The National Museum of African American History and Culture, opened in 2016, traces the story from slavery to civil rights to music and sport.

The National Museum of American History keeps everyday things too: lunchboxes, early computers, a kitchen used by a famous TV chef. The idea is that ordinary objects can explain a country as well as royal treasures.

Most of the Smithsonian's money comes from the US government, with the rest from gifts and its own businesses, such as shops and magazines. That has a side effect. When Congress and the president fail to agree a budget and the government shuts down, the museums can close too, as happened for weeks in 2019 and again in 2025.

Most Smithsonian staff never work in a gallery. Scientists study coral reefs, track birds and name new species. The Smithsonian even runs a research institute in Panama, where scientists study tropical rainforests and the sea creatures on both sides of the Panama Canal. In storerooms the size of aircraft hangars, millions of specimens sit in drawers, waiting for researchers. Some fossils collected a century ago are still revealing new things, the way bones in [[@dino-museums|dinosaur museums]] around the world keep surprising experts.

The National Zoo, also part of the Smithsonian, has bred rare animals and run research on giant pandas for decades. Its pandas have come and gone as agreements with China changed. All of this began with one man's wish to spread knowledge to a country he had only read about.

text: More than 3 crore people live in Greater Tokyo, the area made up of the city and its neighbouring towns. That is more than the population of many countries. Yet streets are clean, crime is low and trains run almost to the second. The city works because of good planning, a huge rail network and people who follow shared habits, such as queuing neatly and keeping quiet on trains.
Tokyo also prepares carefully for disasters. It sits in a part of the world with frequent earthquakes, typhoons and floods, so much of its planning is about staying safe when things go wrong.

myth: Tokyo has always been the capital of Japan.
Kyoto was the capital for over a thousand years, from 794. The emperor moved to Edo in 1868, and the city was renamed Tokyo, meaning "eastern capital".

sec.t:
Tokyo began as a fishing village called Edo. In 1603, the shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu, Japan's military ruler, made it his base. By the 1700s, Edo was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people. [[@kyoto|Kyoto]] remained the emperor's home and Japan's official capital.

In 1868, the emperor moved to Edo, and it was renamed Tokyo, "eastern capital". The city was badly damaged twice in the 1900s, by the Great Kanto Earthquake of 1923 and by bombing in the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]]. Each time it rebuilt.

Japan has many [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]], and Tokyo's buildings are designed for them. [[@skyscrapers|Skyscrapers]] have deep foundations and frames that bend instead of breaking. Some sit on giant rubber pads or shock absorbers that let the ground move beneath them. Tokyo Skytree, 634 m tall, has a central concrete column inspired by the design of old wooden pagodas, which have survived earthquakes for centuries.

Every 1 September, the anniversary of the 1923 earthquake, Japan holds Disaster Prevention Day. Schools and offices practise drills.

Typhoons can dump huge amounts of rain on Tokyo. To protect the city, engineers built one of the world's largest flood [[@tunnels|tunnels]]. Under Saitama, just north of Tokyo, giant shafts collect overflowing river water and send it to a huge tank, 177 m long and about 25 m high, held up by 59 concrete pillars. Pumps then push the water into a bigger river.

Land in Tokyo is expensive, so homes are often small. People make clever use of space with folding furniture and tiny kitchens. The city is full of convenience stores open day and night, and [[@vending-machines|vending machines]] selling drinks on almost every street.

Tokyo is also a capital of pop culture. Districts such as Akihabara are packed with shops selling electronics, games and [[@manga-anime|manga and anime]]. Food is just as important. Tokyo has more restaurants with Michelin stars than any other city, but most people eat in small noodle shops and family restaurants.

sec.h: A city that sorts its rubbish
sec.t: Tokyo stays clean even though there are few public bins. People carry their rubbish home and sort it into types, such as burnable, non-burnable and recyclable, and put each out on its own collection day.

text: Yes. Most of the world's 7,000 or so [[@languages-world|languages]] grew slowly and naturally over thousands of years. But people have invented hundreds of languages on purpose, and a few have real speakers.

The most successful is Esperanto. It was created by Ludwik Lejzer Zamenhof, an eye doctor, and published in 1887. He wanted [[@words-hardest-language|an easy, neutral second language]] that anyone could learn, so people from different countries could talk as equals. He signed his booklet "Doktoro Esperanto", meaning "Doctor Hopeful", and the language took that name.

Other invented languages were made for stories, such as Elvish in [[@tolkien|Tolkien's]] books and Klingon in *Star Trek*. Klingon was built by a language expert, Marc Okrand, with deliberately strange sounds and grammar so it would feel alien. Fans have since translated *Hamlet* into it. And in at least one famous case, a group of children invented a new language without even trying.

st.prompt: In Esperanto, every noun ends in the same letter. Which one?

options.t: -o, as in *hundo* (dog)
-e, as in *hunde*

sec.h: A boy who heard four languages

sec.t:
In English, the past tense of "go" is "went", and of "see" is "saw". Learners have to memorise hundreds of oddities like these. Esperanto has none.

Every noun ends in -o: *hundo* is dog. Every adjective ends in -a: *granda* is big. Verbs end in -as for now, -is for the past and -os for the future: *mi kantas* is "I sing", *mi kantis* "I sang", *mi kantos* "I will sing". Every letter always makes the same sound, so you can read any word aloud correctly once you know [[@alphabet-history|the alphabet]]. "Hello" is *saluton*.

Supporters say this makes Esperanto much quicker to learn than most languages. Critics point out that it is easier mainly for speakers of European languages, since its words come from them.

Esperanto never became the world's second language. Still, it has a green star flag, a world congress held almost every year since 1905, thousands of books and songs, and speakers on every continent. UNESCO passed resolutions supporting it in 1954 and 1985. Since 2015, millions of people have tried free online courses in it.

Estimates of how many people speak it well vary hugely, from tens of thousands to about two million. A few families use it at home, so it even has native speakers.

The most surprising invented language had no single inventor. In Nicaragua in the late 1970s and 1980s, new schools brought together hundreds of deaf children who had never been taught a [[@sign-language|sign language]]. They began signing to each other on buses and in playgrounds.

Over a few years, their gestures turned into a full language with its own grammar, now called Nicaraguan Sign Language. Younger children who joined made it richer and more regular. Scientists studied it closely, because it showed something rarely seen: a brand-new human language being born.

text: Cotton grows on a bushy plant. After it flowers, it forms a green pod called a boll. When the boll ripens, it splits open and a ball of soft white fibres puffs out, clinging to the seeds inside.

Farmers pick the fluffy bolls. A machine called a gin pulls the seeds out. The fibres are cleaned and combed straight, then twisted into long threads, which is called spinning. The threads are woven or knitted into cloth, then dyed or printed. A pair of [[@jeans|jeans]] or a school uniform is the end of that long chain.

sec.t:
Each cotton fibre is a single plant cell, grown long and thin from the skin of a seed. In the wild, the fluff helps seeds float away on the wind or drift on water.

The fibres are mostly cellulose, the same stuff that makes paper. Under a microscope, a dried cotton fibre looks like a flat, twisted ribbon. Those natural twists help fibres grip each other when they are spun, which is why cotton makes strong, soft thread that soaks up sweat.

People in South Asia were among the first to spin cotton. Archaeologists at Mehrgarh, in present-day Pakistan, found cotton threads inside a copper bead about 7,000 years old. In the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]], people grew cotton and wore woven cloth.

For thousands of years, Indian cotton cloth was famous around the world. Fine muslin from Dhaka was so light that it was compared to woven air. Calico from Calicut and chintz prints were traded to Rome, Arabia and later Europe.

For most of history, all this work was done by hand. A small roller gin, called a charkhi in India, squeezed seeds out of the fibre. Then spinners twisted fibres into yarn on a spindle or a spinning wheel.

The thread was woven on a loom. Long threads called the warp are stretched tight, and the weaver passes another thread, the weft, over and under them. The pattern of over and under decides whether the cloth is plain, twilled like denim, or patterned.

In the 1920s, [[@gandhi|Mahatma Gandhi]] asked Indians to spin their own thread on a charkha and wear handwoven [[@khadi|khadi]] instead of British mill cloth. Spinning became a sign of self-reliance during the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]]. The charkha even appeared on an early version of the Indian flag.

India and China are now the world's largest cotton growers, and Texas grows the most in the United States. Growing cotton can use a lot of water and pesticides, so some farmers are trying new methods. A cotton T-shirt is simple to wear, but it carries a very long story.

text: Paan is a fresh, heart-shaped betel leaf wrapped around a filling and chewed after a meal. The classic version holds slices of areca nut, called *supari*, a smear of wet lime paste and a dab of *kattha*, a reddish paste from tree bark. Sweet paan swaps in rose jam, fennel seeds, coconut and cherries.

People across South and Southeast Asia have chewed paan for at least 2,000 years. It is offered to guests, served at weddings and placed before gods. But its most common ingredients, areca nut and tobacco, are a major cause of mouth cancer, so doctors warn against them.

sec.h: A leaf with a long history
sec.t:
Old Sanskrit writings call paan *tambula*, and describe it as a sign of hospitality and luxury. Kings handed paan to visitors as a mark of honour. Accepting a paan from someone could seal a promise.

In the 1300s, the Moroccan traveller [[@ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] described the betel leaf in India and how prized it was. Under the Mughals, paan became an art. Nobles carried silver boxes called *paandaan* with tiny bowls for each filling. Folding a perfect paan, tight enough to hold together and small enough to pop in whole, became a skill people boasted about.

The betel vine is a climber in the pepper family, related to the plant that gives us [[@cardamom-pepper|black pepper]]. Farmers grow it under shady sheds of bamboo and dried grass, called *barejas*, because the leaves scorch in strong sun. Some betel gardens look like dim green rooms, cool and damp inside.

Different regions grow leaves with different flavours. Banarasi paan from [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] received a GI tag in 2023. Mahoba in Uttar Pradesh is famous for its *desawari* leaf. The Magahi leaf of Bihar is prized for being soft enough to melt in the mouth. Leaves are sold in bundles and wrapped in damp cloth to stay fresh. A skilled paan seller can fold dozens an hour, often pushing a clove through the top like a pin to hold each one shut.

The World Health Organization's cancer research agency lists areca nut as a substance that causes cancer in humans. Chewing it for years, especially with tobacco, raises the risk of mouth cancer sharply. India has one of the highest rates of mouth cancer in the world, and paan with tobacco is one big reason.

Areca nut also stains teeth, wears them down and stiffens the inside of the cheeks over time. Many families now serve only sweet paan without supari or tobacco, made with gulkand, fennel and coconut. A sweet paan with no supari and no tobacco keeps the fun of the tradition without its biggest dangers.

The old custom of offering paan to guests survives at many [[@weddings-india|Indian weddings]], where a paan stall is often the busiest corner after dinner. And the spices folded inside, from cardamom to cloves, carry their own story of sea voyages and fortunes, one that begins with the great [[@spices|spice trade]].

text: A watermelon is a giant water balloon built by a plant. The vine spreads its leaves across the ground and catches sunlight. Through [[@photosynthesis|photosynthesis]], the leaves turn sunlight, air and water into sugar. That sugar, plus huge amounts of water drawn up by the roots, pours into the growing fruit.

Inside the fruit, cells don't just multiply. They also swell, like tiny balloons filling at a tap. Once a flower is pollinated, a typical watermelon goes from marble-sized to ripe in roughly five or six weeks, sometimes gaining a good fraction of a kilo in a day.
Most of what you crunch into is water, about 92%. The rest is mainly sugar, fibre and the red pigment lycopene, the same one that colours tomatoes.

sec.t:
Wild watermelons first grew in Africa. For a long time people thought the ancestor was a bitter melon from southern Africa. A study of watermelon DNA published in 2021 pointed instead to a melon from Sudan, in the north-east, called the Kordofan melon. Its flesh is pale and fairly sweet.

People in the Nile valley were growing watermelons more than 4,000 years ago, and paintings of them appear in Egyptian tombs. Over centuries, farmers chose the sweetest, reddest fruits for seed. Traders carried them to India, China and, after 1492, the Americas.

Today China grows well over half the world's watermelons. In north India, farmers have long grown *tarbooz* on the sandy beds of rivers like the Ganga and Yamuna. They plant in the dry weeks before the monsoon, when the water drops and leaves the banks bare.

The 159 kg record holder was grown by Chris Kent of Tennessee and weighed in 2013. Contest growers use special seed, give each vine plenty of room and space, and often pinch off all but one fruit so the plant puts everything into it. They water carefully, because a sudden flood of water after a dry spell can make a big melon split.

An ordinary market watermelon weighs more like 5 to 10 kg. That's still heavy enough to need two hands and a strong shopping bag.

sec.h: Seeds, no seeds and square ones
sec.t:
Seedless watermelons aren't made with chemicals or tricks. In the 1930s, the Japanese scientist Hitoshi Kihara found a way to cross two kinds of watermelon plant so that the fruit can't form proper seeds. You may still see soft white seed coats inside. Growers plant normal seeds nearby so bees can bring in pollen.

In [[@japan-culture|Japan]], some farmers grow watermelons inside glass boxes so they come out square. They stack neatly in a fridge, but they're often picked before they are ripe and sold as decorations.

In hot weather, a watermelon is a good way to take in [[@water-drink|water]] without a glass. Street sellers in India stack them on carts in April and May. In the American South, a cold slice is a classic July picnic. Either way, every bite is mostly rain and river water that a plant spent the summer collecting.
